name: Abdur Razzaq visits Vijayanagara
what: The Timurid envoy from Herat describes seven rings of walls and a city “such that the pupil of the eye has never seen a place like it”.

sources.cite: Eaton, R. M. 2005. A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761. Cambridge University Press

name: Akapana platform built at Tiwanaku
what: The great terraced platform-mound with its sunken court is raised at the heart of the city.

sources.cite: Janusek, J. W. 2008. Ancient Tiwanaku. Cambridge University Press

name: Angkor Wat begun
what: Suryavarman II starts the temple-mausoleum dedicated to Vishnu; work goes on for about 35 years.

sources.cite: Coe, M. D. 2003. Angkor and the Khmer Civilization. London: Thames & Hudson

name: Bayon built at Angkor Thom
what: Jayavarman VII, the Buddhist king who retook Angkor from the Cham, builds the Bayon with its many stone faces at the heart of his new walled city.

sources.cite: Coe, M. D. 2003. Angkor and the Khmer Civilization. London: Thames & Hudson

name: Cahokia abandoned
what: The city has emptied; floods, drought, soil exhaustion and political breakdown are all proposed.

sources.cite: Pauketat, T. R. 2009. Cahokia: Ancient America’s Great City on the Mississippi. New York: Viking

name: Cahokia’s palisade built
what: A wooden stockade with bastions, rebuilt four times, encloses the central precinct: a sign of rising conflict.

sources.cite: Pauketat, T. R. 2009. Cahokia: Ancient America’s Great City on the Mississippi. New York: Viking

name: Chola raid on Srivijaya
what: Rajendra I’s fleet sacks Srivijaya’s ports on Sumatra and the Malay peninsula and captures its king, breaking its hold on the Straits.

sources.cite: Coedès, G. 1968. The Indianized States of Southeast Asia. Honolulu: East-West Center Press
Wolters, O. W. 1967. Early Indonesian Commerce: A Study of the Origins of Srivijaya. Ithaca: Cornell University Press

name: Kanem at its height under Dunama Dabbalemi
what: Kanem expands north to the Fezzan and keeps a hostel for its pilgrims in Cairo; the ruler is said to have opened the sacred mune.

sources.cite: Lange, D. 2004. Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa. Dettelbach: Röll
Niane, D. T. (ed.) 1984. General History of Africa IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century. UNESCO (chapters on Kanem-Bornu and the East African coast)

name: Gedi abandoned
what: The stone town of Gedi, with its palace and great mosque, is abandoned, probably after Oromo raids and a falling water table.

sources.cite: Horton, M. and Middleton, J. 2000. The Swahili: The Social Landscape of a Mercantile Society. Oxford: Blackwell

name: Great Enclosure walls raised at Great Zimbabwe
what: The largest dry-stone enclosure in sub-Saharan Africa, with its conical tower, goes up over about a century.

sources.cite: Pikirayi, I. 2001. The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States. Walnut Creek: AltaMira

name: Great Zimbabwe declines
what: The capital empties as power moves north to Mutapa and south-west to Khami; overgrazing, drought and shifting gold routes are the usual explanations.

sources.cite: Pikirayi, I. 2001. The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States. Walnut Creek: AltaMira

name: Mai Hummay of Kanem embraces Islam
what: The Girgam chronicle of the Sayfawa dynasty dates the ruler’s conversion to the late eleventh century.

sources.cite: Lange, D. 2004. Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa. Dettelbach: Röll
Levtzion, N. and Hopkins, J. F. P. (eds) 1981. Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History. Cambridge University Press

name: Husuni Kubwa palace built at Kilwa
what: Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman builds a palace with a bathing pool and warehouses on the cliff above the harbour, the largest building south of the Sahara in its day.

sources.cite: Chittick, N. 1974. Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast. Nairobi: British Institute in Eastern Africa

name: Idris Alooma rules Bornu
what: The mai buys Ottoman muskets, campaigns against the Bulala and the Hausa, and is described by his imam Ibn Furtu.

sources.cite: Lange, D. 2004. Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa. Dettelbach: Röll
Niane, D. T. (ed.) 1984. General History of Africa IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century. UNESCO (chapters on Kanem-Bornu and the East African coast)

name: Kedukan Bukit inscription
what: The oldest dated Old Malay text records a victorious expedition (siddhayatra) by the Srivijayan ruler, near Palembang.

sources.cite: Coedès, G. 1968. The Indianized States of Southeast Asia. Honolulu: East-West Center Press
Wolters, O. W. 1967. Early Indonesian Commerce: A Study of the Origins of Srivijaya. Ithaca: Cornell University Press

name: Monks Mound begun
what: The first stages of the largest earthen mound in the Americas (30 m high) go up at Cahokia.

sources.cite: Pauketat, T. R. 2009. Cahokia: Ancient America’s Great City on the Mississippi. New York: Viking

name: Kingdom of Mutapa founded
what: Nyatsimba Mutota leads a move north to the Zambezi valley and founds the Mutapa state, which the Portuguese later knew as Monomotapa.

sources.cite: Pikirayi, I. 2001. The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States. Walnut Creek: AltaMira
Niane, D. T. (ed.) 1984. General History of Africa IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century. UNESCO (chapters on Kanem-Bornu and the East African coast)

name: Pamalayu expedition
what: Kertanegara of Singhasari sends a Javanese expedition to Malayu (Jambi), a sign that Srivijaya’s power has passed to Java.

sources.cite: Coedès, G. 1968. The Indianized States of Southeast Asia. Honolulu: East-West Center Press

name: Portuguese sack of Mombasa
what: Francisco de Almeida’s fleet storms and burns Mombasa weeks after taking Kilwa.

sources.cite: Horton, M. and Middleton, J. 2000. The Swahili: The Social Landscape of a Mercantile Society. Oxford: Blackwell

name: Sack of Vijayanagara
what: After the defeat at Talikota the capital is looted for months by the sultanates’ armies and never reoccupied as a capital.

sources.cite: Fritz, J. M. and Michell, G. 2011. Hampi Vijayanagara. Mumbai: Jaico
Eaton, R. M. 2005. A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761. Cambridge University Press

name: Sayfawa court moves west of Lake Chad to Bornu
what: Driven out of Kanem by the Bulala, the dynasty re-founds itself in Bornu.

sources.cite: Niane, D. T. (ed.) 1984. General History of Africa IV: Africa from the Twelfth to the Sixteenth Century. UNESCO (chapters on Kanem-Bornu and the East African coast)
Lange, D. 2004. Ancient Kingdoms of West Africa. Dettelbach: Röll

name: Tiwanaku state collapses
what: Building stops, the raised fields are abandoned and the colonies break away during a long dry period.

sources.cite: Kolata, A. L. 1993. The Tiwanaku: Portrait of an Andean Civilization. Oxford: Blackwell
Janusek, J. W. 2008. Ancient Tiwanaku. Cambridge University Press

name: Vasco da Gama finds a pilot at Malindi
what: Rebuffed at Mombasa, da Gama is welcomed by the ruler of Malindi, who gives him a Gujarati pilot for the crossing to Calicut.

sources.cite: Subrahmanyam, S. 1997. The Career and Legend of Vasco da Gama. Cambridge University Press

name: Vijayanagara founded
what: The brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family found a new capital on the Tungabhadra, by tradition on the advice of the sage Vidyaranya.

sources.cite: Eaton, R. M. 2005. A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761. Cambridge University Press

name: Yijing studies at Srivijaya
what: The Chinese monk stops six months in Srivijaya to learn Sanskrit on the way to Nalanda, and later spends years there copying texts (687-695).

sources.cite: Coedès, G. 1968. The Indianized States of Southeast Asia. Honolulu: East-West Center Press

name: Zheng He’s fleet on the Swahili coast
what: Ships of the fifth Ming treasure voyage (1417-1419) call at Mogadishu, Barawa and Malindi and return with envoys and a giraffe.

sources.cite: Dreyer, E. L. 2007. Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty, 1405-1433. New York: Pearson Longman

name: Zhou Daguan at Angkor
what: A Yuan envoy spends a year in Angkor and writes the only eyewitness account of daily life in the Khmer capital.

sources.cite: Zhou Daguan, A Record of Cambodia: The Land and Its People, trans. P. Harris. 2007. Chiang Mai: Silkworm
Coe, M. D. 2003. Angkor and the Khmer Civilization. London: Thames & Hudson

name: Mapungubwe
what: Hilltop capital at the Limpopo-Shashe confluence, the first state on the southern African plateau; famous for its gold rhinoceros.
why: Its rise and fall (perhaps with a drier climate) passed the gold trade north to Great Zimbabwe.

sources.cite: Huffman, T. N. 2007. Handbook to the Iron Age. Pietermaritzburg: University of KwaZulu-Natal Press
Pikirayi, I. 2001. The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States. Walnut Creek: AltaMira
